item.title: Could That Burn Be Worse Than It Looks?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Burns in dogs are deceptive injuries — what looks like minor redness in the first few minutes can reveal itself as a much deeper wound a day or two later
  • The four main types — thermal, chemical, electrical, and mechanical — each call for slightly different responses
  • Burn severity depends on both depth and surface area, since widespread shallow burns can cause major fluid and protein loss and lead to systemic illness even when the wound looks less dramatic
  • Emergency first aid means cool water (not cold or icy) for 15 to 20 minutes, a loose nonstick covering, warmth for transport, and a fast call to the veterinarian
  • Even small-looking burns deserve a vet's eye, since the depth of injury may not be visible right away

Your dog leans against the wood stove for half a second. Your puppy nibbles a phone charger cord. A cup of hot coffee tips off the coffee table and lands on a curious nose. Whatever the scene, the panic hits fast — and what your dog's skin looks like in the first few seconds does not always tell the whole story.

Burns are deceptive injuries. The visible damage can be subtle at first, even when deeper layers of skin and tissue are seriously hurt. That is why even a small-looking burn deserves a careful look, and often a phone call to your veterinarian.

Why Burns Are So Easy to Underestimate

With most cuts and scrapes, what you see is more or less what you get. Burns do not play by the same rules. The skin's full response to a burn can take hours — sometimes days — to show up. Surface redness may not look alarming, but the tissue underneath can already be damaged.

That delayed reveal is especially true of thermal burns, where heat continues to penetrate even after the source is gone. By the time blisters form or the skin starts to darken, the burn has been quietly worsening below the surface. The early window for limiting damage is short.1,2

The 4 Main Types of Burns in Dogs

Most burns in dogs fall into one of four categories, and the type matters because the right response is not always the same. Here is what sets them apart:3,4

  • Thermal burns — They come from house fires, stoves, hot liquids, steam, hot pavement, sunburn, or radiant heat sources like wood stoves. These are by far the most common.
  • Chemical burns — They are brought on by contact with bleach, drain cleaners, battery acid, paint thinners, gasoline, or other harsh substances.
  • Electrical burns — Pets that chew on cords, become exposed to live wires, or when water becomes in contact with an electrical source. Mouth burns from cord-chewing puppies are a recognized type. Electrical burns can often lead to a dangerous build-up of fluid in the lungs, so the burns in the mouth are just the beginning.
  • Mechanical or friction burns — These result from friction, like rope burns, carpet burns, pavement burns, or leash burns when a dog drags or is dragged across a surface.

Knowing which type you are dealing with helps the veterinarian choose the right treatment — and in the case of chemical burns, it can change the very first step you take at home.

Severity Depends on 2 Factors

Burns are classified by how deep they go and how much of the body they cover. A small, very deep burn and a wide, shallow burn can both be dangerous, just in different ways. Burns covering a large surface area can cause major fluid and protein loss, leading to systemic illness even when the burn is not especially deep.5 In veterinary medicine, burn depth is classified under three categories:6,7,8

  • Superficial burns (first-degree) affect only the top layer of skin, the epidermis. You will see redness, swelling, fur loss, and tenderness. These typically heal in a few days with simple care.
  • Partial-thickness burns (second-degree) reach into the dermis, the second layer of skin. They are painful, often blistered, and may ooze or weep. These take a few weeks to a few months to heal and carry a real risk of infection.
  • Full-thickness burns (third-degree) destroy all layers of skin and the fatty tissue underneath. The area can look red, white, or charred and leathery black.

Because the nerve endings are destroyed, these burns can paradoxically feel less painful — which is one of the reasons they are easy to underestimate. Healing takes months, often requires surgical debridement or skin grafts, and leaves permanent scarring.

Emergency First Aid: What to Do (and What Not to Do)

If your dog has been burned, the first minutes count. Stay calm, and work through these steps in order:9,10

  1. Check the basics first — Make sure your dog is breathing and responsive, and call for emergency help if they are not. If you have been trained in pet CPR, this is where you use it.
  2. Cool the burn with cool (not cold) water — Run cool tap water over the area for about 15 to 20 minutes. This eases pain and helps stop heat from continuing to penetrate the deeper layers of skin. For a single burned body part, you can immerse it in cool water. Do not immerse a dog with widespread burns, as cooling too much skin too quickly can trigger shock.
  3. Cover the area gently — Place a clean, moist cloth or a sterile, non-adherent dressing loosely over the burn. The goal is to protect the wound from contamination, not to wrap or compress it.
  4. Keep your dog warm — especially with larger or deeper burns — A blanket draped over your dog during transport helps prevent hypothermia, which can sneak up quickly when significant skin is damaged.
  5. Use a muzzle if it is safe to do so — Even gentle, easygoing dogs can react unexpectedly when in pain. A makeshift muzzle from gauze or a soft leash can keep both of you safer on the way to the clinic.

Call your veterinarian or bring your pet to the emergency clinic immediately. Burns can worsen rapidly beneath the surface, and the sooner a professional sees the injury, the better the outcome. However, some old-school remedies actually make burns worse. Avoid the following:

  • Do not apply butter, petroleum jelly, oil, or human ointments — they can trap heat, contaminate the wound, and some are toxic to dogs.
  • Do not use ice or ice water — extreme cold can worsen tissue damage and cause hypothermia.
  • Do not pop or drain blisters — intact skin over a blister is actually protective.
  • Do not apply tight bandages. A loose, nonstick covering is what you want.
  • Do not immediately flush a chemical burn with water without checking first. Some chemicals react badly with water — look up the substance or call animal poison control before pouring.
  • Do not use peroxide, harsh soaps, or household disinfectants on a burn.

Does Every Burn Need a Vet?

Any burn that is deep, large, near the face or eyes, on the paw pads, or caused by a chemical or electrical source needs same-day veterinary care.

Even smaller, surface-level burns are worth a call to your veterinarian. As mentioned, what looks superficial in the first few minutes can reveal itself to be deeper a day or two later. A veterinarian can assess the depth of injury, prescribe appropriate pain control and antibiotics if needed, and give you specific instructions for at-home care.11

What Treatment Looks Like at the Clinic

Treatment depends on the type, depth, and extent of the burn. For mild burns, your veterinarian may simply clean the area, apply a topical treatment, and give you home-care instructions.

For more serious burns, treatment becomes more involved. IV fluids are often given to replace the fluids lost through damaged skin. Blood or plasma transfusions may be needed if protein loss is severe. Pain management is critical, since burns are notoriously painful — your veterinarian may use a combination of injectable and oral medications. Antibiotics are commonly prescribed for partial- and full-thickness burns to prevent infection.

Bandaging and topical treatments are tailored to the stage of healing, and bandages typically need to be changed daily under sterile conditions. For full-thickness burns, debridement and sometimes skin flaps or grafts may be needed to close the wound.

Dogs unable to stand may need help with positioning and nutritional support, since healing burns demand a lot of calories.12

Ongoing Care at Home

Once your dog is home, the work is not over. Your veterinarian will give you a specific care plan, but a few general principles apply:13,14,15

  • Watch closely for signs of infection — Increasing redness, swelling, warmth, foul odor, or discharge are all reasons to call back. Keep an eye out for areas turning black or leathery, which can signal the formation of eschar (dead tissue) that may need to be removed.
  • Keep your dog from licking, scratching, or chewing the area — A recovery cone or medical pet shirt can help. If bandages are part of the care plan, keep them clean and dry, and let your veterinarian handle the bandage changes when possible.
  • Only use topical products your veterinarian specifically recommends — Some over-the-counter options that work well for humans can be harmful to dogs, and others may slow healing rather than help it.

Reducing the Risk in the First Place

You cannot bubble-wrap every household risk, but a few habits can lower the odds of a burn happening in the first place. Take note of these safety reminders:

  • Use stove guards, fireplace screens, and baby gates to keep dogs at a safe distance from heat sources
  • Keep the kitchen a pet-free zone while cooking, especially with hot oil or boiling water
  • Run the hose for a minute before letting your dog drink — sun-warmed water inside the hose can reach scalding temperatures
  • Puppy-proof electrical cords and outlets — chewing on cords can cause mouth and palate burns, and lead to life-threatening pulmonary edema
  • Store bleach, drain cleaners, and other harsh chemicals well out of reach
  • Use dog-safe sunscreen on light-coated or thinly furred breeds
  • Watch hot pavement in summer — if the back of your hand cannot rest on the ground for seven seconds, it is too hot for paws

The Bottom Line

Dog burns can look minor in the moment and turn out to be much more serious as the hours unfold. Stay calm, cool the area gently, cover it loosely, skip the kitchen-cabinet remedies, and call your veterinarian — even for burns that seem small.

Most dogs recover beautifully from minor burns with prompt, calm care. The deeper or more widespread ones demand veterinary expertise and patience. Either way, your fast response and a clear-headed plan are what tilt the odds toward a smooth recovery and skin that heals as well as it can.

Sources and References

  • 1,3,7,12,14 VCA Animal Hospitals, Burns in Dogs
  • 2,4,8,10,11,15 American Kennel Club, October 7, 2025
  • 5 DVM360, August 1, 2008
  • 6,9,13 American Red Cross, Burns in Dogs

item.title: This Pet Crisis Needs Urgent Action, but Don’t Ignore These Other 13 Signs
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Since your dog can’t tell you when she’s sick or in pain, it’s important to always be on alert for signs of potential health problems
  • There are several signs that should trigger a call to your veterinarian, including new lumps and bumps on your dog’s body, noticeable weight gain or loss, and bleeding or unusual discharge
  • Other signs include a persistent cough, stiffness or limping, and difficulty breathing
  • Sudden collapse is always a medical emergency — even if your dog recovers quickly, all reasons for fainting or collapsing require an immediate veterinary visit
  • Excessive drinking, panting, scratching and urination are signs of underlying conditions ranging from bladder infections and metabolic disorders to cancer

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published March 27, 2019.

When dogs don't feel well, or there's reason to suspect as much, it would be such a relief if they could just say so, wouldn't it? It's incredibly stressful to have a dog who, for example, is clearly miserable judging by her hunched posture, tucked tail and sad eyes, and there's no way to gauge what's going on, how long it might last or how serious it is.

Even if you’re very disciplined about taking your dog for regular veterinary checkups, it’s still very important to be alert for changes in her health or behavior between visits. After all, you know your furry best friend better than anyone, and you’re her first line of defense when there’s a problem brewing beneath the surface.

14 Common Health Warning Signs in Dogs

The Morris Animal Foundation lists common signs to watch for in dogs that should always prompt a call to your veterinarian.1

  1. Skin lumps or bumps — Most of the time, lumps and bumps on a dog’s skin are harmless, though they can be unsettling and ugly. However, it’s important to have new growths evaluated by your veterinarian. It's rare that a growth requires emergency action, however, occasionally a mass like an abscess or cyst may require urgent care.

    If you find a growth on your pet’s body, keep a close eye on it to see whether it changes or grows over time. If it begins growing quickly or shows noticeable changes, have your veterinarian evaluate it as soon as possible. However, if you notice, for example, a discoloration on the skin or what looks like a skin tag that doesn't get bigger or change over the course of days, weeks or months, then just mention it to your vet at your pet's next wellness exam.
  2. Sudden collapse — this is an emergency! — When a dog collapses, it means he experiences a sudden loss of strength that causes him to fall and not be able to get back up. If a collapsed dog also loses consciousness, he has fainted. Either of these situations is an emergency, even if your dog recovers quickly and seems normal again within seconds or minutes of the collapse.

    All the reasons for fainting or collapsing are serious and require an immediate visit to your veterinarian. They include a potential problem with the nervous system (brain, spinal cord or nerves), the musculoskeletal system (bones, joints, muscles), the circulatory system (heart, blood vessels, blood) or the respiratory system (mouth, nose, throat, lungs).
  3. Dramatic weight gain or loss — If your dog seems to be gaining a lot of weight, it’s most likely a result of what she’s eating (e.g., a dry diet), how much she’s eating and a lack of physical activity (most dogs — no matter their size or age — don’t get nearly the exercise they need).

    However, it’s also possible that a tumor in her abdomen can make your dog appear to be gaining weight or getting fat, so it’s best to give your veterinarian a call if your dog is getting bigger and you don’t know why.

    On the flip side, often a loss of appetite is the first sign of an underlying illness in dogs. There can be many reasons your dog isn’t hungry or refuses to eat, but not eating can begin to negatively impact his health within 24 hours. And for puppies 6 months or younger, the issue is even more serious.

    Weight loss is the result of a negative caloric balance, and it can be the consequence of anorexia (loss of appetite) or when a dog’s body uses or eliminates essential dietary nutrients faster than they are replenished. Weight loss exceeding 10% of your dog’s normal body weight will be a red flag for your veterinarian. There can be several underlying causes, some of which are very serious.
  4. Changes in chewing, eating and drinking habits — If your dog is having difficulty chewing, there’s something painful going on in his mouth that needs investigating. Possibilities include dental or gum disease, a broken tooth or tooth resorption.

    Changes in your dog’s appetite or eating habits can signal any number of underlying problems, from oral disease to a gastrointestinal (GI) disorder to cancer. If your dog is suddenly drinking his water bowl dry, it’s also cause for concern. Excessive thirst (along with excessive urination) are symptoms of several disorders, including urinary tract problems and kidney disease.
  5. Non-healing sores or wounds — If your dog has a sore or wound that isn’t healing, the most immediate concerns are pain and the potential for infection. There are many nontoxic therapies that can successfully treat these wounds, including manuka honey, negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT), shockwave therapy and laser therapy.

    Since sores that won’t heal can also be a sign of a more serious underlying disease such as cancer, schedule an appointment with your veterinarian for diagnosis and treatment.
  6. Loss of energy — A lethargic dog will appear drowsy, “lazy” and/or indifferent. She may be slow to respond to sights, sounds and other stimuli in her environment. Lethargy or exhaustion is a non-specific symptom that can signal a number of potential underlying disorders, including some that are serious or life-threatening. If your pet is lethargic for longer than 24 hours, it’s time to make an appointment with your veterinarian.
  7. Bleeding or discharge from any orifice — “Orifices,” or openings into and out of your dog’s body, include the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, anus and urethra. If you notice bleeding or unusual discharge from any of these openings, make an appointment with your veterinarian. Be aware that digested blood in your dog’s poop will appear as black tarry stools. Fresh blood in the stool indicates bleeding in the colon or rectum. Either situation is cause for concern and should be investigated as soon as possible.

    Blood in your dog’s urine, called hematuria, can be obvious or microscopic. There are a few serious disorders that can cause bloody urine, including a blockage in the urinary tract, a bacterial infection and even cancer. Vomited blood can be either bright red (fresh) or resemble coffee grounds (indicating partially digested blood). There are a variety of reasons your dog might vomit blood, some of which are relatively minor, but others are serious and even life-threatening.
  8. Persistent cough — Coughing in dogs, unless it’s a one-and-done situation, generally indicates an underlying problem. Examples include a possible windpipe obstruction, kennel cough, bronchitis, pneumonia, heartworm disease, heart failure, and tumors of the heart and lungs. All causes of coughing require investigation, and in most cases, treatment.
  9. Change in breath or body odor — A common cause of stinky breath in dogs is dental or gum disease, which is entirely preventable in many cases. If your pet’s mouth has reached the point of emitting a foul odor, it’s past time to make an appointment with your veterinarian for an oral exam.

    Poor skin and coat condition can cause unpleasant body odor in dogs, as can a yeast infection. If your pet’s normal “doggy smell” suddenly turns sour, give your veterinarian a call.
  10. Persistent lameness, stiffness or limping — Mobility problems in dogs are always a sign of an underlying, often painful condition such as arthritis. There are many things you and your veterinarian can do to either resolve or effectively manage the disorders that inhibit your dog’s ability to move around comfortably, so it’s important to have him seen by your vet as soon as possible.
  11. Difficulty breathing, urinating or defecating — A dog in respiratory distress will have labored breathing or shortness of breath that can occur when he breathes in or out. Breathing difficulties can mean that not enough oxygen is reaching his tissues. Additionally, dogs with heart failure may not be able to pump enough blood to their muscles and other tissues.

    Respiratory distress often goes hand-in-hand with a buildup of fluid in the lungs or chest cavity that leads to shortness of breath and coughing. If your dog has sudden undiagnosed breathing problems or appears to be breathing harder, heavier or faster than before, he should see a veterinarian immediately.

    Difficulty urinating includes discomfort while urinating, straining to urinate and frequent attempts to urinate with little success. If your dog cries out while relieving himself, seems preoccupied with that area of his body or is excessively licking the area, you should make an appointment with your veterinarian right away. There are several underlying causes of urinary difficulties, some of which can result in death within just a few days.

    Your dog should poop at least once every day because it’s an important part of his body’s natural detoxification process. He’s constipated when he either has difficulty pooping (and the stool he produces is dry and hard), or he isn’t pooping at all. This is why it’s so important to keep an eye on those daily “deposits.” The quantity, color, texture and smell, along with the presence of mucus or blood in your pet’s feces (and urine), are all indicators of his general well-being.

    Often, what passes from (or in the case of constipation, doesn’t pass from) your pet’s body is the first sign of a health problem, so you should regularly monitor your dog's potty area and familiarize yourself with what “normal” looks like for your pet.

    On potty walks, constipated dogs tend to look like they’re trying to go or need to go, but nothing’s happening. If after a few minutes of hunching and straining your dog doesn’t go or produces poop that is small, hard and dry, you can reasonably assume he’s constipated.

    Sometimes constipated dogs appear bloated and painful, especially when trying unsuccessfully to poop. The stool a constipated dog does manage to pass is often darker than normal and may contain mucus, blood or strange debris. If your dog seems constipated, make an appointment with your veterinarian so she or he can check for underlying conditions.
  12. Vomiting or diarrhea — Unless your dog vomits or has a bout of diarrhea as the result of eating something she shouldn’t have, which you have identified, it’s cause for concern. Chronic vomiting or diarrhea are red flag signs of an underlying problem that requires your veterinarian’s attention.
  13. Eating more than normal — If your dog suddenly becomes food-obsessed (or more food-obsessed than usual), a relatively unlikely but serious possibility is the presence of an underlying medical condition that causes excessive hunger, no matter how much he eats.

    Schedule an appointment with your veterinarian if your dog seems to be extra hungry even though he's eating well, and especially if he's also losing weight.
  14. Excessive drinking, panting, scratching or urination — A brewing bladder infection, other types of infection, a metabolic problem such as Cushing's disease and diabetes can cause excessive thirst and water consumption. Some forms of cancer cause pets to drink more. If your dog is drinking more water than normal, you should have her checked by your veterinarian to rule out an underlying condition.

  • There are several signs that should trigger a call to your veterinarian, including new lumps and bumps on your dog’s body, noticeable weight gain or loss, and bleeding or unusual discharge

  • Excessive drinking, panting, scratching and urination are signs of underlying conditions ranging from bladder infections and metabolic disorders to cancer

When dogs don't feel well, or there's reason to suspect as much, it would be such a relief if they could just say so, wouldn't it? It's incredibly stressful to have a dog who, for example, is clearly miserable judging by her hunched posture, tucked tail and sad eyes, and there's no way to gauge what's going on, how long it might last or how serious it is.

Even if you’re very disciplined about taking your dog for regular veterinary checkups, it’s still very important to be alert for changes in her health or behavior between visits. After all, you know your furry best friend better than anyone, and you’re her first line of defense when there’s a problem brewing beneath the surface.

14 Common Health Warning Signs in Dogs

The Morris Animal Foundation lists common signs to watch for in dogs that should always prompt a call to your veterinarian.1

  1. Skin lumps or bumps — Most of the time, lumps and bumps on a dog’s skin are harmless, though they can be unsettling and ugly. However, it’s important to have new growths evaluated by your veterinarian. It's rare that a growth requires emergency action, however, occasionally a mass like an abscess or cyst may require urgent care.

  2. Sudden collapse — this is an emergency! — When a dog collapses, it means he experiences a sudden loss of strength that causes him to fall and not be able to get back up. If a collapsed dog also loses consciousness, he has fainted. Either of these situations is an emergency, even if your dog recovers quickly and seems normal again within seconds or minutes of the collapse.

    All the reasons for fainting or collapsing are serious and require an immediate visit to your veterinarian. They include a potential problem with the nervous system (brain, spinal cord or nerves), the musculoskeletal system (bones, joints, muscles), the circulatory system (heart, blood vessels, blood) or the respiratory system (mouth, nose, throat, lungs).
  3. Dramatic weight gain or loss — If your dog seems to be gaining a lot of weight, it’s most likely a result of what she’s eating (e.g., a dry diet), how much she’s eating and a lack of physical activity (most dogs — no matter their size or age — don’t get nearly the exercise they need).

    However, it’s also possible that a tumor in her abdomen can make your dog appear to be gaining weight or getting fat, so it’s best to give your veterinarian a call if your dog is getting bigger and you don’t know why.

    On the flip side, often a loss of appetite is the first sign of an underlying illness in dogs. There can be many reasons your dog isn’t hungry or refuses to eat, but not eating can begin to negatively impact his health within 24 hours.     Weight loss is the result of a negative caloric balance, and it can be the consequence of anorexia (loss of appetite) or when a dog’s body uses or eliminates essential dietary nutrients faster than they are replenished.   4. Changes in chewing, eating and drinking habits — If your dog is having difficulty chewing, there’s something painful going on in his mouth that needs investigating. Possibilities include dental or gum disease, a broken tooth or tooth resorption.

    Changes in your dog’s appetite or eating habits can signal any number of underlying problems, from oral disease to a gastrointestinal (GI) disorder to cancer. Excessive thirst (along with excessive urination) are symptoms of several disorders, including urinary tract problems and kidney disease.
  5. Non-healing sores or wounds — If your dog has a sore or wound that isn’t healing, the most immediate concerns are pain and the potential for infection. There are many nontoxic therapies that can successfully treat these wounds, including manuka honey, negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT), shockwave therapy and laser therapy.

    Since sores that won’t heal can also be a sign of a more serious underlying disease such as cancer, schedule an appointment with your veterinarian for diagnosis and treatment.
  6. Loss of energy — A lethargic dog will appear drowsy, “lazy” and/or indifferent. She may be slow to respond to sights, sounds and other stimuli in her environment. Lethargy or exhaustion is a non-specific symptom that can signal a number of potential underlying disorders, including some that are serious or life-threatening. If your pet is lethargic for longer than 24 hours, it’s time to make an appointment with your veterinarian.
  7. Bleeding or discharge from any orifice — “Orifices,” or openings into and out of your dog’s body, include the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, anus and urethra.     Blood in your dog’s urine, called hematuria, can be obvious or microscopic. There are a variety of reasons your dog might vomit blood, some of which are relatively minor, but others are serious and even life-threatening.

Chronic vomiting or diarrhea are red flag signs of an underlying problem that requires your veterinarian’s attention.
  13. Eating more than normal — If your dog suddenly becomes food-obsessed (or more food-obsessed than usual), a relatively unlikely but serious possibility is the presence of an underlying medical condition that causes excessive hunger, no matter how much he eats.

item.title: Did Your Pup's Dinner Take a Wrong Turn?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Megaesophagus is a condition where the esophagus loses its muscle tone and ability to move food into the stomach — instead of digesting normally, food and water pool in the tube and come back up as passive, undigested regurgitation
  • Regurgitation is not the same as vomiting — there is no heaving or warning, and the food often appears in a tube-like shape because it never reached the stomach
  • The condition comes in two forms: congenital (present at birth, showing up around weaning) and acquired (developing later in life, often secondary to myasthenia gravis, Addison's disease, vascular ring anomalies, esophagitis and inflammatory bowel disease, or other underlying issues)
  • Aspiration pneumonia occurs when regurgitated food or water slips into the lungs; it is the leading cause of death in dogs with megaesophagus, which is why early diagnosis and careful feeding matter so much
  • Feeding in an upright position (often with a Bailey chair), adjusting food consistency, offering small frequent meals, and staying upright for 10 to 30 minutes after eating can dramatically improve quality of life for affected dogs

Your dog finishes their bowl, walks a few steps, and — without any heaving or warning — a tube-shaped pile of undigested food appears on the floor. It happens after breakfast or dinner. Sometimes it happens hours later, and sometimes water comes back up too.

If this scene is becoming familiar, your dog's dinner may literally be taking a wrong turn. A condition called megaesophagus could be the reason food is not reaching the stomach the way it is supposed to — and the sooner you understand what is going on, the better the outcome tends to be.

What Megaesophagus Actually Is

The esophagus is the muscular tube that carries food and water from your dog's mouth down to their stomach. When everything works the way it should, the muscles in that tube contract in a coordinated wave — a process called peristalsis — and push each swallow down where it belongs.1

In a dog with megaesophagus, those muscles lose their tone and their coordination. Without that wave of contractions, food and liquid cannot get pushed into the stomach. They sit in the esophagus instead, which stretches and dilates over time. The name itself describes the result — "mega" (large) esophagus.

Megaesophagus is not really a single disease. It is better understood as a combination disorder — the esophagus enlarges and loses motility because of something else going on, whether that is a developmental problem, a neuromuscular issue, or another underlying condition.2,3

Regurgitation Is Not the Same as Vomiting

This distinction matters more than it sounds. Many pet parents (and even some veterinarians, at first glance) can confuse the two — but they point to very different problems. Vomiting is an active process. Your dog heaves, retches, and forcefully ejects what was in their stomach. There are usually warning signs beforehand — drooling, lip licking, and a queasy posture. The contents often include bile because the food made it that far.4,5

Regurgitation is passive. Your dog simply opens their mouth and undigested food or water falls out, often in a tube-like shape that matches the esophagus itself. There is no heaving, no abdominal effort, and usually no bile, because the food was never in the stomach to begin with.6

Megaesophagus is the most common cause of persistent, chronic regurgitation in dogs. If your dog seems to be "throwing up" without effort, that is a clue worth bringing to your veterinarian.7

2 Types of Megaesophagus: Congenital and Acquired

Megaesophagus is not a one-size-fits-all condition, and one of the first things veterinarians try to pin down is when it started. That timing makes a real difference — it points to different likely causes, different treatment paths, and often a different long-term picture. Based on when symptoms first appear, megaesophagus is generally divided into two main categories:8,9,10

  • Congenital megaesophagus is present at birth — Puppies start showing signs around the time of weaning and beginning to eat solid food — they regurgitate, struggle to grow, and seem hungry but uncomfortable.

    Sometimes the underlying issue is a vascular ring anomaly, where a blood vessel near the heart wraps around the esophagus and pinches it during development. Some puppies outgrow congenital megaesophagus as their nervous system matures; others need lifelong management.
  • Acquired megaesophagus develops later in life — It typically occurs in young adult to middle-aged or senior dogs. It is often secondary to another condition — approximately 30% of cases are caused by myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune disease that disrupts the nerve-to-muscle signaling the esophagus depends on. Other causes include dysautonomia, idiopathic, endocrine related (Addison’s disease in particular), and the list goes on.

Common Causes and Breeds at Risk

When megaesophagus is acquired, the underlying trigger is sometimes identifiable and sometimes not. Known causes include:11,12,13

  • Myasthenia gravis — the most common known cause of acquired megaesophagus comprising approximately 25% to 30% of cases14,15 
  • Hormonal conditions like Addison's disease (hypoadrenocorticism) and possibly hypothyroidism (causal link has not been established, but there may be a correlation)
  • Esophageal strictures, foreign bodies, or tumors that block the tube
  • Severe esophagitis (inflammation of the esophagus), which can be an extension of inflammatory bowel disease
  • Neuromuscular disorders like polymyositis, lupus, or polyradiculoneuritis
  • Infectious diseases such as distemper, tetanus, botulism, or neospora
  • Toxins, including lead, snake venom, or certain pesticides
  • Dysautonomia and other nerve-related conditions

When no underlying cause can be found, the condition is called idiopathic megaesophagus — and it is unfortunately not uncommon.

Megaesophagus is more common in dogs than cats, and certain breeds are more prone to it. Hereditary forms have been documented in wire-haired fox terriers and miniature schnauzers. Other breeds that may be predisposed include German shepherds, Great Danes, Labrador retrievers, Golden retrievers, Newfoundlands, Irish setters, Chinese shar-peis, and Greyhounds. Among cats, Siamese cats are considered at higher risk.16,17

Signs to Watch For

Megaesophagus often announces itself in small, easy-to-miss ways before the bigger signs show up. The hallmark sign is regurgitation, but megaesophagus can also bring a cluster of related symptoms that show up alongside it — or sometimes before the regurgitation becomes obvious:18,19,20

  • Passive regurgitation of undigested food or water, often soon after eating
  • Difficulty swallowing or gurgling sounds when they try
  • Excessive drooling
  • Weight loss despite a healthy appetite
  • Bad breath
  • Poor quality hair coat
  • Coughing, nasal discharge, or rapid breathing (signs of aspiration pneumonia)
  • A visible bulge at the base of the neck where the esophagus has stretched
  • Muscle weakness and wasting from chronic undernutrition
  • Acting hungry but picking at food, possibly because eating has become uncomfortable

In puppies, you may also see slow growth and failure to thrive compared to littermates.

The Big Risk: Aspiration Pneumonia

The most dangerous complication of megaesophagus is not the regurgitation itself — it is what can happen during it. Because regurgitation is sudden and passive, the protective reflex that normally closes off the windpipe does not always have time to engage. Food, water, or saliva can slip down into the lungs instead.

That is called aspiration pneumonia, and it is the leading cause of death in dogs with megaesophagus. Signs include coughing, fever, labored breathing, lethargy, and a sudden drop in energy. Aspiration pneumonia is a medical emergency — if you suspect it, your dog needs immediate veterinary care.21,22

How It Is Diagnosed

Most cases of megaesophagus are diagnosed through thoracic radiographs (chest X-rays), which can show the dilated, food- or air-filled esophagus and sometimes a displaced trachea. If the plain radiograph (X-ray) is not conclusive, your veterinarian may use a contrast study with barium or a real-time imaging technique called fluoroscopy to watch the swallowing process in motion.23

Once megaesophagus is confirmed, the next step is usually a search for the underlying cause. That can include blood work, thyroid testing, adrenal function tests, an acetylcholine receptor antibody test for myasthenia gravis, and often endoscopy or muscle biopsies.

If a specific underlying condition is found, treating it sometimes improves esophageal function — though the esophagus does not always bounce back, even with successful treatment of the root cause. For the many cases without a fixable cause, the focus shifts to long-term management. That includes feeding adjustments, careful monitoring, and medications for specific complications when needed.

Mealtime Becomes the Centerpiece

Feeding strategy is the cornerstone of care. The goal is simple: use gravity to do the work that the esophagus can no longer do on its own.

That means feeding your dog in an upright position, with their head and chest at roughly 45 to 90 degrees relative to the floor. They need to stay upright for at least 10 to 15 minutes — and ideally closer to 20 to 30 minutes — after eating, drinking, or taking medication, so food has time to make it down before they lie back down.

Small dogs can sometimes be held upright in your arms. For medium and large dogs, many families use what is known as a Bailey chair — a tall, narrow, high-chair-like seat that keeps the dog in an upright "begging" position during and after meals. Plans for building one are widely available online.

Food consistency also matters, and the right choice varies dog by dog. Some do better with a soupy slurry, others with canned food, and others with soft meatballs that hold together enough to trigger swallowing reflexes. Small, frequent meals are usually easier than one or two big ones. Water can be tricky too — some vets recommend thickened water or gelatin-style "water cubes" to lower the risk of aspiration.

If upright feeding still is not enough, a feeding tube placed directly into the stomach can bypass the esophagus entirely and is often very well tolerated.24,25,26

What the Outlook Looks Like

There is no sugarcoating that megaesophagus is a serious condition. Without diligent management, prognosis can be poor, and aspiration pneumonia and malnutrition are the leading causes of death.

That said, the picture is not all bleak. With early diagnosis, careful feeding, and an attentive partnership with a veterinarian, many dogs can live happy, full lives with this condition. Dogs whose underlying cause can be identified and treated sometimes see real improvement, and those who avoid aspiration pneumonia generally do best of all.

What to Do When Your Pet’s Dinner Comes Back Up

If your dog's dinner keeps making an unwelcome return trip — quietly, without warning, and without any of the usual signs of nausea — do not write it off as a sensitive stomach. Megaesophagus is one of the conditions that hides in plain sight, mistaken for vomiting until someone asks the right questions.

Catching it early, finding any underlying cause, and adapting how mealtimes work at home can change everything for a dog with this condition. With the right care, even a wrong-turn dinner can land where it belongs — and your dog can keep enjoying their bowl, their bed, and their best life.

Sources and References

  • 1,6,8,11,17,18,21,24 American Kennel Club, January 22, 2026
  • 2,4,7,10,13,16,20,22,23,26 VCA Hospitals, Megaesophagus
  • 3,5,9,12,19,25 PetMD, February 3, 2026
  • 14 Veterinary Partner, September 9, 2025
  • 15 Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association, June 15, 2011

How It Is Diagnosed

Most cases of megaesophagus are diagnosed through thoracic radiographs (chest X-rays), which can show the dilated, food- or air-filled esophagus and sometimes a displaced trachea. If the plain radiograph (X-ray) is not conclusive, your veterinarian may use a contrast study with barium or a real-time imaging technique called fluoroscopy to watch the swallowing process in motion.23

Once megaesophagus is confirmed, the next step is usually a search for the underlying cause. That can include blood work, thyroid testing, adrenal function tests, an acetylcholine receptor antibody test for myasthenia gravis, and often endoscopy or muscle biopsies.

If a specific underlying condition is found, treating it sometimes improves esophageal function — though the esophagus does not always bounce back, even with successful treatment of the root cause. For the many cases without a fixable cause, the focus shifts to long-term management. That includes feeding adjustments, careful monitoring, and medications for specific complications when needed.

Mealtime Becomes the Centerpiece

Feeding strategy is the cornerstone of care. The goal is simple: use gravity to do the work that the esophagus can no longer do on its own.

That means feeding your dog in an upright position, with their head and chest at roughly 45 to 90 degrees relative to the floor. They need to stay upright for at least 10 to 15 minutes — and ideally closer to 20 to 30 minutes — after eating, drinking, or taking medication, so food has time to make it down before they lie back down.

Small dogs can sometimes be held upright in your arms. For medium and large dogs, many families use what is known as a Bailey chair — a tall, narrow, high-chair-like seat that keeps the dog in an upright "begging" position during and after meals. Plans for building one are widely available online.

Food consistency also matters, and the right choice varies dog by dog. Some do better with a soupy slurry, others with canned food, and others with soft meatballs that hold together enough to trigger swallowing reflexes. Small, frequent meals are usually easier than one or two big ones. Water can be tricky too — some vets recommend thickened water or gelatin-style "water cubes" to lower the risk of aspiration.

If upright feeding still is not enough, a feeding tube placed directly into the stomach can bypass the esophagus entirely and is often very well tolerated.24,25,26

What the Outlook Looks Like

There is no sugarcoating that megaesophagus is a serious condition. Without diligent management, prognosis can be poor, and aspiration pneumonia and malnutrition are the leading causes of death.

That said, the picture is not all bleak. With early diagnosis, careful feeding, and an attentive partnership with a veterinarian, many dogs can live happy, full lives with this condition. Dogs whose underlying cause can be identified and treated sometimes see real improvement, and those who avoid aspiration pneumonia generally do best of all.

What to Do When Your Pet’s Dinner Comes Back Up

If your dog's dinner keeps making an unwelcome return trip — quietly, without warning, and without any of the usual signs of nausea — do not write it off as a sensitive stomach. Megaesophagus is one of the conditions that hides in plain sight, mistaken for vomiting until someone asks the right questions.

Catching it early, finding any underlying cause, and adapting how mealtimes work at home can change everything for a dog with this condition. With the right care, even a wrong-turn dinner can land where it belongs — and your dog can keep enjoying their bowl, their bed, and their best life.

item.title: What This 90,000-Dog Study Reveals About Purebred Versus Mixed Breed Health
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Many people, including some veterinarians, believe mixed breed and “designer” dogs tend to be healthier than purebreds
  • Other veterinarians and the results of a 2013 university study suggest mixed breeds don't necessarily have an advantage when it comes to genetic disorders
  • According to the study, the prevalence of 13 of 24 genetic disorders was about the same for mixed breeds and purebreds
  • The field of nutrigenomics studies the effect of nutrition on the genome, and at some point in the future, gene expression will be shaped through personalized nutrition plans
  • It can be helpful for pet parents to learn their mixed breed dog’s ancestry and health predisposition, and work with an integrative veterinarian to prevent or effectively manage inherited diseases

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published April 3, 2019.

Are mixed breed dogs healthier than purebreds? The answer depends on who you ask. A working definition of 'purebred' is helpful here. In the U.S., a dog is considered a pedigreed purebred if she or he:

  • Has papers proving mom and dad and all his or her ancestors are of the same breed
  • Is registered with the American Kennel Club (AKC)

Purebred dogs are the result of selective breeding by humans. So are hybrid or “designer” dogs, which despite their often-high price tags, aren’t technically purebreds. Hybrids are initially created by breeding two or more purebred dogs. For example, Goldendoodles and Labradoodles, two very popular hybrids, were initially created by breeding Poodles with either golden or Labrador retrievers.

Some breeders have gone on to breed purebred-to-hybrid (e.g., a golden retriever to a Goldendoodle) and hybrid-to-hybrid (e.g., a Doodle to a Doodle), creating second or third- or fourth-generation hybrids. This practice is highly controversial in the dog world, for lots of reasons.

Mixed breed dogs, in contrast, are the offspring of dogs of different breeds and breed mixes, and humans may, but usually don’t have a hand in their creation. Often their ancestry isn’t known, and DNA testing can reveal a wide and often improbable range of breeds in their lineage.

It Just Makes Sense That Mutts Are Healthier Than Purebreds — or Does It?

Now back to the question of whether mixed breeds are healthier than purebreds. One of the reasons for this belief is that when two or more breeds are blended in one dog, it can be reasonably assumed there’s less risk the dog will inherit breed-specific diseases.

The idea that mutts are healthier makes sense when you consider the terrible breeding practices of puppy mill operators and many AKC-associated breeders as well.

Sadly, in the world of puppies-for-profit and pedigreed dogs, there is often a single-minded focus on breeding animals for certain physical characteristics — even when those characteristics cause lifelong suffering — and little to no attention paid to selecting for health and longevity.

With that said, according to what many veterinarians see in their practices,1 as well as the results of a 15-year study of veterinary cases at the University of California, Davis, mixed breeds don't necessarily have an advantage when it comes to genetic disorders.2

Certain Genetic Disorders Affect Purebreds and Mixed Breeds Equally

The UC Davis researchers analyzed the records of over 90,000 purebred and mixed breed dogs that had been patients at the university’s veterinary medical teaching hospital between 1995 and 2010. Designer dogs were included in the study, since crossbreeding is presumed to reduce or eliminate genetic disorders like hypothyroidism, epilepsy, hip dysplasia and cancer.

The research team found over 27,000 records that involved dogs with at least one of 24 genetic disorders, including various types of cancers, heart disease, endocrine system dysfunction, orthopedic conditions, allergies, bloat, cataracts, eye lens problems, epilepsy and liver disease.

According to their study results, the prevalence of 13 of the 24 genetic disorders was about the same for purebreds as mixed breeds. Some of those disorders were hip dysplasia, hyper- and hypoadrenocorticism (Cushing’s and Addison’s, respectively), cancers, lens luxation and patellar luxation (floating kneecap).

Ten conditions were found more frequently among purebred dogs, including dilated cardiomyopathy, elbow dysplasia, cataracts and hypothyroidism. One disorder was actually more common in mixed breeds — cranial cruciate ligament (CCL) disease.

“Overall, the study showed that the prevalence of these genetic disorders among purebred and mixed-breed dogs depends on the specific condition," animal physiologist Anita Oberbauer, Ph.D., professor and chair of the Department of Animal Science at UC Davis and lead author of the study said in a university press release.3 The UC Davis study data also suggests breeds that share a similar lineage are more prone to certain inherited disorders:

“… [F]our of the top five breeds affected with elbow dysplasia were the Bernese mountain dog, Newfoundland, mastiff and Rottweiler — all from the mastiff-like lineage. This suggests that these breeds share gene mutations for elbow dysplasia because they were descended from a common ancestor.”

The flip side of the coin is disorders that occur in both mixed breeds and purebreds trace back to well-established gene mutations that have spread throughout the dog population. These disorders include hip dysplasia, tumor-causing cancers and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Nutrition and Genetics

It’s very important to keep in mind that just because a certain disorder is inherited in certain breeds, it doesn’t mean your dog of that breed is fated to acquire that condition. As noted above, there are steps pet owners can take to help prevent your pet from acquiring diseases to which he may be predisposed, and there are ways to successfully treat or effectively manage existing genetic conditions.

For example, nutrigenomics is an emerging scientific concept that holds that the nutrition needed by each individual (both humans and animals) depends on their genetic makeup. Genes and their expression are controlled by individual nutrients, which means personalized functional nutrition is essential.

It’s important to understand how the nutrients fed to pets will affect their genes, and therefore, their health and longevity. And in fact, knowing which nutrients are essential for individual pets (and people) can impact longevity, reduce the risk of chronic disease and heal from illness much more rapidly.

Nutrigenomics studies the effect of nutrition on the genome. The genome is everything to do with the body — how it functions metabolically and genetically. The genes are only a small part of the genome, about 2%. The other 98% has nothing to do with the genes, but with how the body controls what the genes do.

Every individual has a unique molecular dietary signature that determines which nutrients that individual should eat in order to thrive. As veterinarians and pet parents, there is some control here. For example, if your dog is a breed genetically predisposed to a certain health problem, through nutrition certain genes can be suppressed so they don't express themselves, or other genes encouraged to do the opposite.

For more information on this exciting field of research, consider the book co-written by Dr. Jean Dodds, “Canine Nutrigenomics: The New Science of Feeding Your Dog for Optimum Health.”

If You’re Looking for More Info on Your Dog’s Breed(s)

If you're interested in learning more about inherited diseases in dogs, there are a couple of online resources you may find useful:

  • The Canine Inherited Disorders Database (CIDD) is a good resource for dog guardians with a pet diagnosed with an inherited disease, and prospective dog parents who want to learn about the inherited conditions of certain breeds.
  • The Inherited Diseases in Dogs (IDID) database is provided by the University of Cambridge Veterinary School, and users can search by selecting a breed or genetic anomaly (inherited disorder), or by typing in a keyword. This database also contains references to peer-reviewed scientific literature for further research.

There are also now DNA test kits available that provide not just breed identification, but health and genetic traits as well. Two of these are the Embark Breed & Ancestry Identification, Trait & Health Detection Dog DNA Test Kit and the Wisdom Panel Health Breed & Health Identification Dog DNA Test Kit.

If you purchase one of these kits, reviewing the results with your veterinarian is strongly recommended, especially if there’s anything you feel is concerning. It can be helpful for pet parents to be aware of the disorders that are common in their dog's breed(s), because in integrative veterinary medicine in particular, there are steps that can be taken to prevent or slow the progression of disease.

When an inherited disorder can't be prevented or develops suddenly, if you know ahead of time what to look for and seek immediate veterinary care, your dog often has a much better outcome.

  • 1 VetStreet, April 18, 2013
  • 2 Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association, June 1, 2013, Vol. 242, No. 11, Pages 1549-1555
  • 3 UC Davis Press Release, May 28, 2013

item.title: The Purple Veggie Most Pet Parents Overlook
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Eggplant contains bioactive compounds such as chlorogenic acid. Research suggests that this compound may help improve insulin resistance, as well as fight inflammation and fight against colitis
  • Rich in phenolics, eggplant contains delphinidin and pectin in the skin that may bind with heavy metals preventing absorption
  • The quercetin in eggplant may help manage inflammation and fight against diabetic neuropathy, as well as lipid peroxidation
  • Other nutrients are present in eggplant, such as manganese, which may help support energy and protein metabolism. The potassium in eggplant may also help with muscle and nervous system function
  • Eggplant can be served in various ways to your pet; both chopped and pureed forms work well

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published July 11, 2024.

The common eggplant is known for its deep purple color and flavor that works well both as a side dish and main course. From baked to fried and boiled, the possibilities of eggplant are endless. The best thing is that your pet can partake in this cherished vegetable as well. However, before you offer it to your pet, learn how to properly prepare and cook it to ensure they reap its benefits.

Did You Know?

Ancient Italians were originally wary of eggplant. They called it “mala insana,” which roughly translates to “mad apples,” as they thought eating it would drive them insane.1,2

Health-Boosting Bioactive Compounds in Eggplant

“Eggplant contains an array of bioactive compounds, namely phenolics, that may benefit pet health. In fact, it contains the most phenolics among the cultivated members of the nightshade family.”3

Eggplant is particularly rich in quercetin, which is known for its anti-inflammatory properties, as well as anticarcinogenic and antiviral capabilities. It may even help inhibit lipid peroxidation and platelet aggregation, as well as stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis, according to a study published in 2016.4 In another analysis, quercetin helped protect kidneys from diabetic nephropathy.5

Another phenolic found in eggplant is chlorogenic acid.6 Similar to quercetin, chlorogenic acid has anti-inflammatory properties and may even attenuate colitis severity, according to one study.7 In another example, chlorogenic acid also helped with glucose tolerance and insulin resistance using a mice model.8 It was also found to be effective against diabetic nephropathy.9

Other bioactive compounds in eggplant include delphinidin, a purple-colored pigment that gives eggplant its striking color. Interestingly, the very same compound may also benefit your pet’s gut microbiota.10 Moreover, the pectin found in eggplant’s skin may bind with heavy metals in the digestive tract to prevent absorption.11

Other Nutrients in Eggplant May Support Pet Health

Eggplant is a good source of manganese,12 a mineral that plays various roles in your pet’s body functions. According to researchers from Oregon State University, manganese is important for energy and protein metabolism, and a deficiency may lead to slow bone growth.13 Another study noted that manganese may help with brain development and neurotransmitter synthesis.14

Eggplant also contains potassium and vitamin K,15 both of which play important roles in pet health. Potassium is important for muscle function,16 as well as for the cardiac and nervous systems.17 Meanwhile, vitamin K is noted for its coagulant properties that may help with blood clotting.18 Vitamin K also plays a role in bone reabsorption19 and maintaining proper bone density.20

Top Producers of Eggplant

New Jersey is the top producer of eggplant in the U.S., with around 849 acres of land dedicated to cultivation. Second place belongs to California, which only has 144 acres devoted to eggplant.21

The Lowdown on Eggplant’s Safety for Pets

Misinformation about many healthy fruits, vegetables, nuts and seeds abounds on the internet. This is because websites have labeled all risks (such as the risk of overconsumption causing gastrointestinal issues, or choking on too large of pieces or pits) as "toxicities," which isn't true but has managed to confuse millions of pet lovers, nonetheless.

In the case of eggplant, there’s a myth that it’s poisonous to pets, but fortunately, that isn’t the case. This vegetable is safe for pets to consume. Eggplant does contain a moderate amount of oxalates,22 an antinutrient that can be problematic for some predisposed animals if the vegetable is consumed in large quantities. All toppers, treats and bowl add-ins should constitute no more than 10% of daily calories, so the amount of eggplant in your pet’s diet will be minimal. To reduce oxalates, if warranted, peel and boil the eggplant.23

Eggplant Fun Fact

Eggplant is generally prepared as a vegetable, but did you know it’s actually classified as a fruit? That’s because eggplant actually grows from the flowers and contains seeds inside as well.24

Selecting and Serving Eggplant to Your Pet

When you’re out in the market for eggplant, look for those with a shiny, smooth skin. Dull skin may indicate poor storage. Wrinkled skin is another sign to watch out for, as it indicates the eggplant is old. The flesh should also be slightly firm.25 You can serve eggplant to your pet raw or cooked, in pureed form (great for lick mats or as a meal topper) or chopped into bite-sized pieces as a training treat.

Sustainability of Eggplant Farming

Eggplant is included in the Environmental Working Group’s Dirty Dozen list.26 This means conventionally grown varieties contain pesticide residues. If possible, look for organic, spray-free eggplants, as these are eco-friendly and do not contain toxic pesticides.

In a study published in 2021, researchers noted that organic farming of eggplant produced a 24.15% lower total environmental footprint compared to conventional yields. Ecotoxicity due to conventional eggplant farming practices, particularly the use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides, was also 83% higher than organic practices’ ecotoxicity.27 If you’re unable to buy organic eggplant, conventional eggplant is still OK. Just make sure to wash it thoroughly before cooking it for your meals and/or feeding it to your pet.

The Lowdown on Eggplant’s Safety for Pets

Misinformation about many healthy fruits, vegetables, nuts and seeds abounds on the internet. This is because websites have labeled all risks (such as the risk of overconsumption causing gastrointestinal issues, or choking on too large of pieces or pits) as "toxicities," which isn't true but has managed to confuse millions of pet lovers, nonetheless.

In the case of eggplant, there’s a myth that it’s poisonous to pets, but fortunately, that isn’t the case. This vegetable is safe for pets to consume. Eggplant does contain a moderate amount of oxalates,22 an antinutrient that can be problematic for some predisposed animals if the vegetable is consumed in large quantities. All toppers, treats and bowl add-ins should constitute no more than 10% of daily calories, so the amount of eggplant in your pet’s diet will be minimal. Eggplant is generally prepared as a vegetable, but did you know it’s actually classified as a fruit? That’s because eggplant actually grows from the flowers and contains seeds inside as well.24

When you’re out in the market for eggplant, look for those with a shiny, smooth skin. Dull skin may indicate poor storage. Wrinkled skin is another sign to watch out for, as it indicates the eggplant is old. The flesh should also be slightly firm.25 You can serve eggplant to your pet raw or cooked, in pureed form (great for lick mats or as a meal topper) or chopped into bite-sized pieces as a training treat.

Sustainability of Eggplant Farming

Eggplant is included in the Environmental Working Group’s Dirty Dozen list.26 This means conventionally grown varieties contain pesticide residues. If possible, look for organic, spray-free eggplants, as these are eco-friendly and do not contain toxic pesticides.

In a study published in 2021, researchers noted that organic farming of eggplant produced a 24.15% lower total environmental footprint compared to conventional yields. item.title: Spending Too Much on Pet Care? 3 Ways to Cut Back
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • In 2016, U.S. pet owners are expected to spend $62.75 billion on their pets, which is 4% more than what was spent in 2015
  • Preventive veterinary care and a fresh, species-appropriate diet are two areas worth splurging on in your pet care budget
  • Areas to save on in your pet expenses include grooming, as you can trim nails and give baths at home, and certain toys
  • Pets don't need clothing and costumes — items like Halloween costumes, raincoats and boots are typically unnecessary and may hinder your dog's ability to move freely and naturally
  • Pet ownership saves Americans $11.7 billion annually in health care costs, primarily in the form of reduced doctor visits, according to a study conducted for the HABRI Foundation

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published September 17, 2016.

In 2016, U.S. pet owners are expected to spend $62.75 billion on their pets, which is 4% more than the $60.3 billion spent in 2015.1

The data, collected by the American Pet Products Association (APPA), shows a continued trend: spending on pet care has risen every year since the APPA began collecting such data in 1994.2

Broken down, the APPA data suggests it costs more than $1,600 a year to care for a dog and more than $1,100 to care for a cat. Food makes up the most expensive part of caring for a pet, followed by veterinary care, supplies and services, such as grooming and boarding.

Most pet owners view their pets as part of the family, and many spare no expense when it comes to their pet.

Virtually every family has a budget, and pet care expenses shouldn’t push you continually into the red. (The exception may be if your pet has an accident or sudden illness, and the emergency treatment or surgery puts you temporarily over your budget.)

When considering where to splurge and where to save money on your pet, there are definite areas that deserve more spending than others.

Pet Care Saving Versus Spending

When caring for an animal, an ounce of prevention is truly worth a pound of cure. By spending your pet care dollars wisely, you can actually save money by reducing your pet’s future veterinary care costs. Here are examples of how to best allocate your funds.

  • Splurge: Preventive veterinary and dental care — Preventive health care involves regular monitoring of your pet’s health status and taking proactive steps as necessary to prevent the development of disease. This isn’t a one-size-fits-all approach; it should be tailored to your individual pet’s needs.

    Your pet should be seen at least once a year for a regular check-up. However, if she is older or has a chronic health condition, a check-up with a proactive, functional medicine vet every six months is wise.

    You’ll be able to check on things like organ function and make changes in your pet’s treatment protocol, to prevent more serious issues from occurring.

    Checking your pet’s internal organ function is one of the best investments, as it can identify organ dysfunction before your pet goes into organ failure, and provides you the opportunity to address the problem you otherwise wouldn’t have known about.

    Keep in mind that you do not need to vaccinate your pet on an annual schedule, either. Proactive vets advocate the use of vaccine titers in place of unnecessary, repeated vaccines.

    In addition, keeping your pet’s mouth healthy will help keep her body healthy, as there’s an intricate link between oral health and overall health.

    It's worth learning how to brush your pet's teeth and doing it consistently (daily if your pet is older or at least several times a week for younger pets). Oral exams will be included in your proactive wellness physical examination, to check for other issues that may be occurring in your pet’s mouth.
  • Splurge: Feed a fresh, balanced species-appropriate diet — This is one of the most important tools to keep your pet healthy and, in turn, lower your veterinary costs in the future.

    You’ll want to avoid feeding highly processed, high-carbohydrate and low-moisture foods (including most commercial kibbles, “grain-free”/high-starch dry food, and low-quality canned foods).

    This type of junk-food diet is the opposite of what your pet is designed to eat, and feeding such foods to your pet will lead to significant metabolic and physiologic stress. Instead, choose a fresh-food diet that is close to what your pet would eat in the wild.
  • Save and splurge: Toys — Your pets need toys for mental stimulation and physical play, but you don’t need to break the bank to buy them. Some of the best toys can be made at home or are free (like re-purposing cardboard boxes for your kitty).

    Also, many dogs destroy new toys in a matter of minutes, which may prompt you to buy cheap toys. Be careful with purchasing low-quality toys, including those made from plastic, which may contain harmful chemicals (flame retardants), questionable fillers or break apart easily, posing a choking hazard.

    If you are going to buy toys, be on the lookout for those made of 100% natural rubber, organic cotton or other nontoxic materials. Some of the best pet toys are locally produced, usually handmade by small business owners using all organic or natural materials. Another option to save some money is to make old toys new again. Leave out only one or two at a time and put the rest away for a week or two. When you pull them out, they'll be like new.
  • Save: Clothing and costumes — Pets don’t need (nor do many enjoy) wearing extravagant clothing and costumes. Items like hooded sweatshirts, Halloween costumes, raincoats and boots are typically unnecessary and, in some cases, may hinder your dog’s ability to move freely and naturally.

    That being said, some dogs, particularly small or toy breeds, those with short or thin coats, older dogs, or those with chronic health conditions, may benefit from wearing a sweater or coat in cold weather. For this purpose, choose a plain sweater or coat with no zippers, hooks or buttons that may annoy your dog (or pose a choking hazard) in a natural material (organic if possible).
  • Save: Nail trims and baths — Taking your pet to the groomer can be pricey. It’s necessary to keep your pet’s nails trimmed, but you can learn to do so yourself.

    The same goes for bath time. You needn’t shell out a lot of money for pet baths. Bathing your dog (and sometimes even your cat) at home will save you money and be less stressful for your pet.

It’s interesting to note that while having a pet does cost you money, it also saves you money on your own health care costs. In fact, researchers from George Mason University (GMU) conducted a study for The Human-Animal Bond Research Initiative (HABRI) Foundation, which found Americans save $11.7 billion annually in health care costs due to pet ownership, primarily in the form of reduced doctor visits.3

Of course, even with the inevitable spending on pet care, there’s no price that can be put on the “return on your investment” — the love and companionship of an animal.

Sources and References

  • U.S. News & World Report August 21, 2024
  • 1 APPA, Industry Market Size & Ownership Statistics
  • 2 Fortune August 26, 2016
  • 3 HABRI December 14, 2015

item.title: Why Does Your Dog Hide Their Favorite Things?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Hiding and burying favorite things is one of the most universal canine behaviors — and it traces back thousands of years to your dog's wild ancestors
  • The instinct made sense in the wild because cool, dark soil functioned as a natural refrigerator, kept the scent away from other predators, and gave the hunter's family a safe stash to return to later
  • Certain breeds are especially prone because digging and stashing instincts stem from their hunting heritage; rescue dogs often hide food too, sometimes from earlier scarcity and sometimes as a self-soothing habit
  • Hiding is usually harmless, but it can cross into compulsive territory or expose pets to unsafe chemicals and debris
  • Dogs should never be allowed to eat what they dig out of the ground, since decomposing food can cause stomach upset, vomiting and diarrhea

You reach under the couch cushion for the remote and pull out a soggy rawhide. A favorite chew toy has gone missing for the third time this week, only to turn up tucked inside the laundry basket. Out in the yard, a fresh mound of dirt marks the spot where the new bone disappeared yesterday.

If this sounds familiar, you are not alone. Hiding and burying favorite things is one of the most universal — and most puzzling — dog behaviors. The good news is that there is an apparent reason behind it.

The Instinct Behind the Hiding

Burying and hiding go back thousands of years, long before kibble bowls and squeaky toys. Your dog's wild ancestors — wolves and other early canids — lived a feast-or-famine life. When they made a kill, they ate what they could and hid the rest to protect it from competitors and to save it for leaner days.1

That survival strategy got hard-wired into the canine brain. Even after generations of domestication, the instinct to protect valuable resources by stashing them away is still very much alive in your dog.2

Food Protection in the Wild

For wild dogs, finding food was challenging work. Hunting took time and energy, and a successful kill was a small jackpot. Once they caught their prey, they ate quickly and buried the rest — partly because their stomachs could only hold so much, and partly because other hungry mouths were always nearby.

Pack members would happily steal someone else's dinner if they caught the scent. Big cats, hyenas, jackals, and other predators would too. Tucking the leftovers underground was the safest way to make sure the hunter's family — and only the hunter's family — would get a second meal out of the kill.3

Why Dirt Is Nature's Refrigerator

There is another reason burying made sense: It kept the food from going bad. Direct sunlight makes meat spoil quickly, and the cool earth underground works a lot like a refrigerator. The deeper the hole, the cooler the temperature.

Buried meat is also harder for other animals to find, because the soil masks the scent, and in some cases the organic material in the earth adds a kind of "marinade" that some dogs find appealing later. In short, an underground stash kept food cool, safe, and out of reach until it was needed.4,5

Modern Dogs Still Follow Their Ancestors’ Habits

Your dog is not worried about scarce winters or competing predators. Their dinner shows up reliably, treats appear from the cabinet, and toys are unlimited. But the instinct to save valuables is still present.

So, when your dog grabs a food from their bowl and trots off to drop it behind the couch; or when they carry their new bone outside and start digging, they are doing exactly what their ancestors did.

This is also why dogs hide things that are not food. Toys, socks, slippers, chew bones — and yes, even the TV remote — are all fair game. Anything your dog considers valuable can become a "treasure" worth protecting.6

Why Dogs Hide Things Indoors

If your dog buries in the yard, that's instinct having a natural outlet. But what about the dog who tucks toys under the couch cushion or carries a bully stick to bed?

Dogs in multi-pet households often hide things indoors because they feel they need to protect their stash from another dog in the house, but they cannot get outside to bury it properly. The couch cushion becomes the next-best hiding place.7

Even single-dog households see this. A laundry basket, a bed, or a pile of blankets make a perfectly good hiding spot when there is no dirt available.

Breeds That Are Especially Prone

While almost any dog can develop a stashing habit, some breeds were practically designed for it. Terriers and hounds were originally developed to hunt and dig out small ground dwelling prey. Northern working breeds needed to stash food for survival in harsh winter conditions. These breeds carried those instincts into modern life.

That is why it is more likely for you to see daily digging and stashing behaviors in terriers such as Jack Russell, Cairn, Scottish, and Airedales; hounds such as Dachshunds, Beagles, and Bassets; and Northern working breeds such as Siberian Huskies and Alaskan Malamutes. Although any dog breed or rescue may dig and hide food or toys, in these breeds it is part of their DNA.8

The American Kennel Club (AKC) adds that owners of hunting and working breeds tend to notice this behavior more often than owners of herding or non-sporting breeds, which lines up with the idea that the stashing instinct has roots in the hunt.9

Rescue Dogs and the Hiding Habit

Rescue dogs sometimes hide and bury food more than other dogs, and there are a couple of reasons which may be at play. Dogs who once went hungry — whether as strays, in overcrowded homes, or in shelter environments — may have learned to stash food for later whenever they had the chance. That early survival lesson sometimes sticks around long after meals become dependable.

Digging itself can also be self-soothing for an anxious dog, which is another common thread with rescues. If your newly adopted dog suddenly starts hiding food around the house, this may be a sign of anxiety. Often training, patience and regular routines can help dissipate anxiety and help them adapt to their new home.10

When Hiding Becomes a Problem

For most dogs, hiding and burying is a quirky but harmless part of life. But it can become a problem when it crosses into compulsive territory. In these cases, you may see your dog digging until their paws are raw, or destroying the yard or couch. This happens when the behavior becomes driven by anxiety rather than instinct.

Excessive digging can also expose your dog's paws to lawn chemicals, sharp debris, or pests in the soil. If hiding or digging is starting to look obsessive or causing physical harm, then it is time to loop in your veterinarian or a qualified trainer or behaviorist for help.11,12

The Trouble with Buried Bones

One important caution: Even if your dog stashes a bone like a pro, it is not safe for them to eat what comes back out of the ground. Buried food decomposes, and digging up an old bone or piece of meat days or weeks later can lead to diarrhea, vomiting, or even pancreatitis. If your dog has buried a bone, it is safest to quietly retrieve and dispose of it rather than letting them unearth it later to help prevent potential health issues.13,14

What You Can Do

Since the urge to stash comes from a sense that there is more than enough to protect, you can dial it down by making valued items feel a little less endless. The AKC suggests offering toys one or two at a time and rotating them weekly. This keeps your pet interested and prevents boredom. You also may want to avoid giving your pet bones or chews right after a meal when your dog's belly is already full, as they may be more likely to hide them for later.

If your dog clearly loves the hide-and-seek part, lean into it. Teach a "bury and find" game using blankets or a pile of pillows. Set up a dedicated “dirt box” in the yard where digging is allowed. Use gates or fences to keep the flowerbeds off-limits. Giving your dog a safe outlet for digging satisfies a deep instinct without taking apart your sofa or your garden.15

The Bottom Line

When your dog hides a favorite toy or buries a treat, they are not being sneaky. They are tapping into thousands of years of ancestral wisdom that taught their ancestors to protect what is valuable, save it for later, and do not let the neighbors find out where you put it.

The next time you find a tennis ball stashed in the laundry basket or a chew toy under the bed, take it as a little reminder that your couch-loving companion is still, on some level, the same resourceful animal who once roamed the wild — just with much better snacks and a lot more pillows to choose from.

Sources and References

  • 2,7,8,10,12,14 Whole Dog Journal, June 9, 2026
  • 3,4,6,11,13 VCA Hospitals, Why Do Dogs Bury Bones
